title: Continued fractions of pi and higher roots look random

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Continued fractions of pi and higher roots look random

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In continued fraction representation, square roots are purely repetitive and e shows definite regularity, but pi, cube roots, fourth roots and similar numbers have continued fraction terms that seem essentially random.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But for π, as well as for cube roots, fourth roots, and so on, the continued fraction representations one gets seem essentially random.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 4, “Systems Based on Numbers”; section “Mathematical Constants” (from p. 136), p. 143. Scope: continued fraction expansions of common irrational numbers

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch04-16: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.76

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Terms are directly computable and the square-root periodicity component is rigorously settled. The claims about pi and higher roots can be tested deeply but not resolved asymptotically with current results.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compute long continued fractions and test term frequencies, dependence, growth, and compressibility against explicit stochastic models, while checking the proven periodicity theorem for quadratic irrationals. Results resolve finite-scale appearance but not unrestricted asymptotic randomness.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Random has no canonical model for continued-fraction terms.

Statistical behavior of pi's continued fraction remains largely unproved.

Cube roots form an infinite family.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The contrast Wolfram draws for square roots and for e is settled by classical theorems, and those theorems also prove that cube roots of non-cubes are not eventually periodic. The further statement that the terms for pi and higher roots seem essentially random is an appearance claim about computed prefixes, which public expansions can test and not prove. The bundle is therefore only partly resolved.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use Lagrange's theorem for the periodic continued fractions of quadratic irrationals, and the known regular expansion of e, as the proved half. For pi and for higher roots, test long computed continued-fraction terms for periodicity and for statistical irregularity; a simple pattern would refute 'essentially random,' while non-periodicity alone does not establish randomness.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Non-periodic is weaker than random: a structured but unbounded sequence of partial quotients would satisfy the theorem and fail 'essentially random.'

It is still open whether the continued fraction of pi is unbounded, so computation only probes a prefix.
